edges.effect_quant: Music-based interventions appear to improve some dementia-related outcomes, especially cognition and neuropsychiatric symptoms, but the effect is supportive rather than disease-modifying.
edges.mechanism: Music therapy likely works through preserved emotional and procedural neural networks, increased engagement, and reduced agitation rather than through reversal of neurodegeneration itself. That makes it plausible as a symptom-management intervention even when hard disease outcomes are unchanged.
edges.summary: The best-supported claim is that music therapy can modestly improve cognition and behavioral symptoms in people living with dementia. Meta-analyses of randomized trials generally point in a favorable direction, although the intervention is better viewed as supportive care than as a treatment that changes the underlying course of dementia.
edges.caveats: Trial quality and intervention formats vary widely, from passive listening to structured therapist-led sessions. Benefits are usually measured on symptom scales over short follow-up, so this edge should not be framed as prevention or cure.
